docs.title: vexy-markliff
docs.text: vexy-markliff converts Markdown and HTML documents into XLIFF files that translators can work on, and converts those XLIFF files back into text. It ships as a Python package with a command-line tool of the same name.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
You give it a Markdown or HTML file. It renders Markdown to HTML with markdown-it-py, walks the HTML tree with lxml, and collects every run of visible text. Each run becomes one translation unit in an XLIFF document, tagged with the source and target language codes you choose.

vexy-markliff md2xliff guide.md guide.xlf --source_lang=en --target_lang=de

For this input:

# Guide

Save & quit with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+Q.

the tool writes:

<xliff version="2.1" xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1">
  <file id="file_1" source-language="en" target-language="de">
    <trans-unit id="unit_1" state="new">
      <source>Guide</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_2" state="new">
      <source>Save & quit with</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_3" state="new">
      <source>Ctrl</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_4" state="new">
      <source>+Q.</source>
    </trans-unit>
  </file>
</xliff>

The reverse commands (xliff2md, xliff2html) read such a file and write one <p> element per unit.

docs.title: Current status
docs.text:
Version 1.3 is a deliberately small implementation. Read these limits before you plan a workflow around it:

  • Text is extracted per text node, so inline markup splits a sentence into several units (Save & quit with / Ctrl / +Q. above). The markup itself is not kept.
  • The reverse conversion uses the <source> text of each unit, not the <target>. It produces a flat list of <p> elements for both xliff2md and xliff2html; it does not restore headings, lists or Markdown syntax.
  • The output uses XLIFF 1.2 element names (trans-unit, source-language) under the XLIFF 2.1 namespace. Standard XLIFF 2.1 files that use <unit>/<segment> are read as empty. See XLIFF output.
  • There is no skeleton file, no Format Style (fs:fs) annotation, no sentence segmentation and no two-document mode yet.

The design notes describe the full target behaviour: skeleton files, Format Style attributes, inline <mrk> and <ph> codes, and sentence-level segmentation. They are the specification the code is meant to grow into.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Installation: install the package and check the CLI.
  • Quick start: convert one file each way.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: The package exposes a small API. Everything on this page exists in src/vexy_markliff/ in version 1.3.

docs.title: Top-level names
docs.text:
vexy_markliff.__all__ lists:

Name Kind Defined in VexyMarkliff class vexy_markliff/__init__.py (lazy wrapper) ConversionConfig class vexy_markliff/config.py (lazy import) VexyMarkliffCLI class vexy_markliff/cli.py (lazy import) __version__ string vexy_markliff/__version__.py, generated at build time

ConversionConfig and VexyMarkliffCLI are imported on first access through a module-level __getattr__, so import vexy_markliff stays fast. If __version__.py is missing, __version__ is "unknown".

docs.title: VexyMarkliff
docs.text:
from vexy_markliff import VexyMarkliff

converter = VexyMarkliff(config=None)

The top-level VexyMarkliff is a thin wrapper. On the first method call it imports vexy_markliff.core.converter.VexyMarkliff and forwards every call to it. Any attribute that the wrapper does not define is also forwarded.

The config argument is stored and passed to the core converter, which keeps it as self.config. The 1.3 converter does not read any value from it; language codes come from the method arguments.

docs.title: markdown_to_xliff(content, source_lang="en", target_lang="es") -> str
docs.text: Render content (a Markdown string) to HTML, extract text nodes and return an XLIFF document as a string.

docs.title: html_to_xliff(content, source_lang="en", target_lang="es") -> str
docs.text:
Parse content (an HTML string or fragment), extract text nodes and return an XLIFF document as a string.

Both *_to_xliff methods:

  1. Raise ValidationError("Content cannot be empty") if content is empty or whitespace only.
  2. Raise ValidationError if source_lang or target_lang is not two lowercase ASCII letters.
  3. Wrap any other failure in ConversionError, with the original message appended.

docs.title: xliff_to_html(xliff_content) -> str
docs.text:
Parse an XLIFF string with XLIFFDocument.from_xml and return one <p>…</p> line per unit, joined with newlines. Both methods return the same text. They raise ValidationError("XLIFF content cannot be empty") for empty input and wrap other failures in ConversionError.

from vexy_markliff import VexyMarkliff
from vexy_markliff.exceptions import ConversionError, ValidationError

converter = VexyMarkliff()
try:
    xliff = converter.html_to_xliff("<h1>Title</h1><p>Body</p>", "en", "de")
except ValidationError as error:
    print(f"Bad input: {error}")
except ConversionError as error:
    print(f"Conversion failed: {error}")
else:
    print(converter.xliff_to_html(xliff))

Output:

<p>Title</p>
<p>Body</p>

docs.title: ConversionConfig
docs.text:
from vexy_markliff import ConversionConfig

config = ConversionConfig(source_language="en", target_language="es", split_sentences=True)

A plain class (not a Pydantic model) with three attributes:

Attribute Default Validation source_language "en" Two lowercase letters, else ValueError target_language "es" Two lowercase letters, else ValueError split_sentences True None

ConversionConfig.load(config_path=None) reads a YAML file and passes its top-level keys to the constructor:

source_language: en
target_language: de
split_sentences: false

If config_path is None, the file does not exist, or loading fails for any reason (bad YAML, unknown key, invalid code), load returns a default ConversionConfig() without raising.

Note

The converter accepts a ConversionConfig but does not use it in version 1.3. The CLI has no option to load a configuration file.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
All exceptions live in vexy_markliff.exceptions and derive from VexyMarkliffError, which derives from Exception.

Exception Raised by the 1.3 code VexyMarkliffError Base class only ValidationError Empty content, invalid language code, malformed XLIFF in XLIFFDocument.from_xml, serialization failure in to_xml ConversionError Any failure inside a converter method, wrapping the original error ParsingError MarkdownParser and HTMLParser failures FileOperationError Defined, not raised ConfigurationError Defined, not raised

A ParsingError raised inside a converter method reaches the caller as a ConversionError.

docs.title: Parsers
docs.text: vexy_markliff.core exports MarkdownParser, HTMLParser and the core VexyMarkliff.

docs.title: HTMLParser
docs.text:
HTMLParser().parse(content) returns a dictionary:

from vexy_markliff.core import HTMLParser

HTMLParser().parse('<html><head><title>Hi</title></head><body><p class="x">A <b>B</b> C</p></body></html>')

{
    "segments": [
        {"content": "Hi", "translatable": True, "element": "title"},
        {"content": "A", "translatable": True, "element": "p"},
        {"content": "B", "translatable": True, "element": "b"},
        {"content": "C", "translatable": True, "element": "text"},
    ],
    "structure": {"tag": "html", "attributes": {}, "children_count": 2},
}

Each element's .text becomes a segment tagged with the element name. Each element's .tail (text after its closing tag) becomes a segment tagged "text". Whitespace is collapsed to single spaces and trimmed. structure describes only the root element.

HTMLParser().reconstruct(structured) turns the segment list back into <p> lines.

docs.title: MarkdownParser
docs.text: MarkdownParser creates a markdown_it.MarkdownIt("commonmark", {"breaks": True, "html": True}) instance and enables the table and strikethrough rules. parse(content) renders HTML and hands it to HTMLParser.parse. reconstruct delegates to HTMLParser.reconstruct.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
vexy_markliff.models lazily exports three Pydantic models from vexy_markliff.models.xliff:

Model Fields TranslationUnit id: str, source: str, target: str \| None = None, state: str = "new" XLIFFFile id: str, source_language: str, target_language: str, units: list[TranslationUnit] XLIFFDocument version: str = "2.1", files: list[XLIFFFile]

XLIFFDocument(source_lang="en", target_lang="es", content=None) builds one file with id file_1 from a parser result: every segment becomes a TranslationUnit with id unit_<n>, numbered from 1.

Method Purpose XLIFFDocument.to_xml() Serialize to the XML shown in XLIFF output. Units with a non-empty target get a <target> element. XLIFFDocument.from_xml(xml) Parse XML back into models; reads <target> text and the state attribute. XLIFFDocument.content Property returning the parser-style dictionary built from unit source text. 
from vexy_markliff.models.xliff import TranslationUnit, XLIFFDocument, XLIFFFile

doc = XLIFFDocument(
    files=[
        XLIFFFile(
            id="file_1",
            source_language="en",
            target_language="de",
            units=[TranslationUnit(id="unit_1", source="Hello", target="Hallo", state="translated")],
        )
    ]
)
print(doc.to_xml())

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text:
vexy_markliff.utils holds helpers used by the core modules:

Function Behaviour normalize_whitespace(text) Collapse runs of whitespace to one space and trim. validate_language_code(code) True for two lowercase ASCII letters. validate_file_path(path) True if the path exists and is a file. split_sentences_simple(text) Split on ., !, ?; the punctuation is dropped. Not used by the converter. get_logger(name) Return logging.getLogger(name). setup_logging(level="INFO") Call logging.basicConfig with a fixed format.

split_sentences_simple("Dr. Who? Yes. New sentence.") returns ['Dr', 'Who', 'Yes', 'New sentence'], which shows why it is not wired into the converter.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Version 1.3 is about 1,100 lines of Python in ten modules. This page follows one document through them.

docs.title: Module map
docs.text:
src/vexy_markliff/
├── __init__.py          # lazy VexyMarkliff wrapper, lazy imports, __version__
├── __version__.py       # generated by hatch-vcs at build time (not in Git)
├── cli.py               # VexyMarkliffCLI + main(), Fire entry point
├── config.py            # ConversionConfig, ConversionConfig.load()
├── exceptions.py        # VexyMarkliffError and subclasses
├── utils.py             # whitespace, language-code and logging helpers
├── core/
│   ├── __init__.py      # exports VexyMarkliff, MarkdownParser, HTMLParser
│   ├── converter.py     # VexyMarkliff: the four conversion methods
│   └── parser.py        # MarkdownParser, HTMLParser
└── models/
    ├── __init__.py      # lazy exports of the models
    └── xliff.py         # TranslationUnit, XLIFFFile, XLIFFDocument (Pydantic)

The console script vexy-markliff maps to vexy_markliff.cli:main in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Markdown to XLIFF, step by step
docs.text:
Take "# Hello\n\nThis is **bold** text.\n" with source_lang="en" and target_lang="fr".

  1. Entry. VexyMarkliff.markdown_to_xliff in __init__.py imports core.converter.VexyMarkliff on first use and forwards the call.
  2. Validation. The core converter rejects empty content and checks both language codes with utils.validate_language_code.

  3. Markdown rendering. MarkdownParser.parse renders with markdown-it-py (CommonMark preset, html and breaks on, table and strikethrough enabled):

    <h1>Hello</h1>
<p>This is <strong>bold</strong> text.</p>

  4. HTML parsing. HTMLParser.parse calls lxml.html.fromstring, which wraps the two top-level elements in a <div>. _extract_segments walks the tree and yields:

    [
    {"content": "Hello", "translatable": True, "element": "h1"},
    {"content": "This is", "translatable": True, "element": "p"},
    {"content": "bold", "translatable": True, "element": "strong"},
    {"content": "text.", "translatable": True, "element": "text"},
]

  5. Model building. XLIFFDocument(source_lang="en", target_lang="fr", content=...) creates one XLIFFFile with id file_1 and a TranslationUnit per segment (unit_1 … unit_4, state new).

  6. Serialization. XLIFFDocument.to_xml() builds the <xliff> tree with lxml.etree and returns a pretty-printed string.

The element names collected in step 4 are not written to the XLIFF; the models have no field for them.

docs.title: XLIFF back to text
docs.text:
1. XLIFFDocument.from_xml parses the string and reads trans-unit elements in the …:document:2.1 namespace.
  2. The content property turns units back into segment dictionaries using the source text.
  3. HTMLParser.reconstruct wraps each segment in <p>…</p> and joins them with newlines. MarkdownParser.reconstruct calls the same method.

docs.title: Lazy imports
docs.text: markdown-it-py, lxml and Pydantic are imported only inside conversion methods. The top-level VexyMarkliff class lives in __init__.py so that from vexy_markliff import VexyMarkliff does not import core.converter. models/__init__.py and the package __getattr__ do the same for the models, ConversionConfig and VexyMarkliffCLI.

docs.title: Error flow
docs.text:
ValidationError (empty input, bad language code)   ──► raised directly
anything raised inside the conversion try-block    ──► logged, re-raised as ConversionError

The CLI catches every exception from a conversion and calls sys.exit(1). It also exits with 1 if the input path does not exist, before reading it.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Package Used for markdown-it-py Markdown to HTML lxml HTML parsing, XLIFF building and parsing pydantic XLIFF data models fire CLI pyyaml ConversionConfig.load rich Declared in pyproject.toml; not imported by the 1.3 source

docs.title: Planned architecture
docs.text: The design overview describes the intended pipeline: skeleton files with ###uN### placeholders, Format Style (fs:fs, fs:subFs) annotations, inline <mrk> and <ph> codes, sentence segmentation and a two-document alignment mode.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The vexy-markliff command is a Fire front end to the VexyMarkliffCLI class in vexy_markliff/cli.py. It has four commands. Each reads one file and writes one file.

vexy-markliff md2xliff   INPUT_FILE OUTPUT_FILE [--source_lang=en] [--target_lang=es]
vexy-markliff html2xliff INPUT_FILE OUTPUT_FILE [--source_lang=en] [--target_lang=es]
vexy-markliff xliff2md   INPUT_FILE OUTPUT_FILE
vexy-markliff xliff2html INPUT_FILE OUTPUT_FILE

docs.title: Common behaviour
docs.text:
• Input files are read as UTF-8. Output files are written as UTF-8.
  • The parent directory of OUTPUT_FILE is created if it does not exist. An existing output file is overwritten.
  • On success the command prints nothing and exits with status 0.
  • On any failure the command exits with status 1. A missing input file, empty input or an invalid language code produces no message at all. A parse or conversion error produces one or two log lines on standard error (from Python's logging fallback handler) before the exit. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: md2xliff
docs.text:
Convert a Markdown file to XLIFF.

Argument or flag Short form Default Meaning INPUT_FILE required Path to the Markdown file. OUTPUT_FILE required Path to the XLIFF file to write. --source_lang -s en Source language code. --target_lang -t es Target language code.

Language codes must be two lowercase ASCII letters (en, de, fr). Codes such as EN, en-US or pt_BR are rejected.

vexy-markliff md2xliff README.md build/README.de.xlf -s en -t de

Fire also accepts the hyphenated spellings --source-lang and --target-lang.

docs.title: html2xliff
docs.text:
Convert an HTML file to XLIFF. Arguments and flags are the same as for md2xliff.

vexy-markliff html2xliff index.html index.xlf --source_lang=en --target_lang=fr

HTML fragments work as well as full documents; lxml.html.fromstring accepts both.

docs.title: xliff2md
docs.text:
Convert an XLIFF file produced by md2xliff or html2xliff back to text.

vexy-markliff xliff2md index.xlf index.md

The output is one <p>…</p> line per <trans-unit>, built from the <source> text. The current implementation does not emit Markdown syntax, so xliff2md and xliff2html produce the same output.

docs.title: xliff2html
docs.text:
Convert an XLIFF file back to HTML.

vexy-markliff xliff2html index.xlf index.html

The output has the same shape as for xliff2md. The text is written as-is; characters such as & and < are not re-escaped for HTML.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
Fire generates help from the docstrings:

vexy-markliff --help
vexy-markliff md2xliff --help

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
Status Meaning 0 The output file was written. 1 The conversion failed. Validation failures print nothing; parse errors log to standard error.

Reading other XLIFF files

xliff2md and xliff2html look for <trans-unit> elements in the urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1 namespace. A standard XLIFF 2.1 file that uses <unit> and <segment> yields no units, and the command writes an empty output file with status 0. See XLIFF output.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • uv.
  • Git, with tags fetched (git fetch --tags), because the version is derived from tags.

docs.title: Set up a development environment
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository and enter it:

    git clone https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-markliff.git
cd vexy-markliff

  2. Install the package in editable mode with the development and test extras:

    uv pip install -e ".[dev,test]"

    The dev extra installs pre-commit, ruff, mypy, absolufy-imports, pyupgrade and isort. The test extra installs pytest, pytest-cov and coverage.

  3. Optionally install the Git hooks defined in .pre-commit-config.yaml (whitespace and YAML/TOML checks, ruff, ruff-format, mypy):

    pre-commit install

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
The test suite is in tests/ and runs in well under a second.

uv run --with pytest pytest -q

Or through the Hatch environment defined in pyproject.toml:

uvx hatch run test
uvx hatch run test-cov

test-cov prints a coverage report for src/vexy_markliff and tests.

docs.title: Lint and format
docs.text:
uvx hatch run lint     # ruff check + ruff format
uvx hatch run fix      # ruff check --fix --unsafe-fixes + ruff format
uvx hatch run type-check

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
The root build.sh builds the documentation, the package, or both:

./build.sh            # docs and package
./build.sh docs       # src_docs/md → docs/ with ProperDocs
./build.sh package    # uv build into dist/, then twine check

docs.title: Write documentation
docs.text:
The documentation source is in src_docs/md/; the configuration is src_docs/mkdocs.yml. docs/ holds the generated site that GitHub Pages serves, so do not edit it by hand.

  1. Edit or add Markdown files in src_docs/md/. Add new pages to the nav list in src_docs/mkdocs.yml.

  2. Preview the site:

    src_docs/build.sh serve

    The site is served at http://127.0.0.1:8000.

  3. Build it in strict mode, which fails on any warning such as a broken link:

    src_docs/build.sh

The Docs GitHub workflow runs the same build on every push to main that touches src_docs/ and commits the result to docs/.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
Releases are tagged vX.Y.Z. publish.sh runs gitnextver to commit and tag the next version, builds the package from that tag and uploads it with uv publish. It needs a PyPI token in UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN.

The Release workflow also builds and uploads to PyPI when a v* tag is pushed. It sets skip-existing: true, so it does not fail when publish.sh already uploaded the same version.

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Keep the code small. The 1.3 release removed most of the earlier code base; new features should come with tests and a clear user need.
  • Every source file carries a this_file comment with its path relative to the repository root.
  • Check behaviour against the design notes when you extend the converter, and update them if the design changes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • The runtime dependencies are installed automatically: fire, lxml, markdown-it-py, pydantic, pyyaml and rich.

lxml ships binary wheels for the common platforms. If your platform has no wheel, pip compiles it and needs the libxml2 and libxslt development headers.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
The PyPI package name is vexy-markliff; the import name is vexy_markliff.

uvuv projectpip 
uv pip install vexy-markliff

uv add vexy-markliff

python -m pip install vexy-markliff

To run the CLI once without installing it into an environment:

uvx vexy-markliff --help

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository:

    git clone https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-markliff.git
cd vexy-markliff

  2. Install the package in editable mode with the test extras:

    uv pip install -e ".[test]"

The version number comes from the latest Git tag through hatch-vcs. A commit after the v1.3.1 tag builds as a development version such as 1.3.2.dev0+g1831c684d; a tagged commit builds as the plain tag version.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
1. Print the package version:

    python -c "import vexy_markliff; print(vexy_markliff.__version__)"

    If the version file has not been generated (for example, when you run from a source tree that was never built or installed), this prints unknown.

  2. List the CLI commands:

    vexy-markliff --help

    Fire prints the command group with md2xliff, html2xliff, xliff2md and xliff2html.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text: uv pip uninstall vexy-markliff

docs.title: XLIFF output
docs.text: This page describes the exact XML that version 1.3 writes and reads. It differs from the XLIFF 2.1 standard in ways that matter if you send the files to a CAT tool or translation management system.

docs.title: Document shape
docs.text:
XLIFFDocument.to_xml() builds the tree with lxml and serializes it with pretty_print=True. There is no <?xml …?> declaration.

<xliff version="2.1" xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1">
  <file id="file_1" source-language="en" target-language="fr">
    <trans-unit id="unit_1" state="new">
      <source>Hello</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_2" state="new">
      <source>This is</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_3" state="new">
      <source>bold</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_4" state="new">
      <source>text. Second sentence.</source>
    </trans-unit>
  </file>
</xliff>

That output comes from this Markdown:

# Hello

This is **bold** text. Second sentence.
Element or attribute Value xliff/@version Always 2.1 xliff/@xmlns urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1 file/@id Always file_1 (one file per document) file/@source-language, file/@target-language The language codes you passed trans-unit/@id unit_1, unit_2, … in document order trans-unit/@state new for freshly extracted units source One text node from the input, whitespace collapsed target Written only when a unit has non-empty target text

docs.title: How units are cut
docs.text:
The extractor walks the HTML tree depth first. For each element it emits the element's leading text, then recurses into each child, then emits the child's tail text. Every non-empty piece becomes its own unit.

Consequences:

  • A paragraph with inline markup becomes several units. This is **bold** text. gives This is, bold and text..
  • A paragraph without inline markup stays one unit, however many sentences it has. No sentence splitting is done.
  • Markup is dropped. Link targets, image alt text and all other attributes are not extracted.
  • Code blocks and <script> or <style> contents are extracted like any other text.

docs.title: Differences from XLIFF 2.1
docs.text:
The XLIFF 2.1 core uses the namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0 with version="2.1", the attributes srcLang/trgLang on <xliff>, and the elements <unit> and <segment>. Version 1.3 of vexy-markliff instead writes:

  • XLIFF 1.2 element and attribute names: <trans-unit>, source-language, target-language.
  • state on <trans-unit>; in XLIFF 2.1 state belongs on <segment>.
  • A namespace URI ending in 2.1.

A tool that validates against the XLIFF 2.1 schema will reject these files. The design notes describe the standard structure that the project is meant to produce.

docs.title: Reading XLIFF back
docs.text:
XLIFFDocument.from_xml() parses the XML with lxml and looks for:

  • //xliff:file and .//xliff:trans-unit, with xliff bound to urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1;
  • the source-language, target-language, id and state attributes;
  • the text of the first <source> and <target> child.

Anything else is ignored. A file in another namespace, or one that uses <unit>/<segment>, parses without error but yields zero units.

xliff_to_markdown and xliff_to_html then write one line per unit:

<p>Hello</p>
<p>This is</p>
<p>bold</p>
<p>text. Second sentence.</p>

The <source> text is used even when a <target> exists, so filling in translations and converting back returns the original language. Only the text of <source> itself is read; text inside child elements of <source> is lost.

docs.title: Sample files
docs.text: The documentation site carries a short passage in four localization formats (XLIFF 2.1, PO, Qt TS and RESX) for comparison. See Sample files.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page takes one Markdown file to XLIFF and back, first with the CLI and then from Python.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• vexy-markliff is installed (see Installation).
  • You have a working directory you can write files into.

docs.title: Convert Markdown to XLIFF
docs.text:
1. Create a file named guide.md:

    # Guide

Save & quit with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+Q.

```python
print("hi")
```

  2. Convert it, with English as the source language and German as the target language:

    vexy-markliff md2xliff guide.md out/guide.xlf --source_lang=en --target_lang=de

    The command prints nothing and exits with status 0. It creates the out/ directory if it does not exist.

  3. Open out/guide.xlf:

    <xliff version="2.1" xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1">
  <file id="file_1" source-language="en" target-language="de">
    <trans-unit id="unit_1" state="new">
      <source>Guide</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_2" state="new">
      <source>Save & quit with</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_3" state="new">
      <source>Ctrl</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_4" state="new">
      <source>+Q.</source>
    </trans-unit>
    <trans-unit id="unit_5" state="new">
      <source>print("hi")</source>
    </trans-unit>
  </file>
</xliff>

What happened:

  • markdown-it-py rendered the Markdown to HTML. The raw <kbd> tag passed through because HTML is enabled in the renderer.
  • lxml parsed the HTML. Every non-empty text node and every non-empty tail text after an element became one unit, in document order.
  • The heading, the three pieces of the paragraph and the code block each became a <trans-unit>, numbered unit_1 to unit_5.
  • The & was escaped to & by the XML serializer.

docs.title: Convert XLIFF back to text
docs.text:
vexy-markliff xliff2md out/guide.xlf out/guide-back.md

out/guide-back.md now contains:

<p>Guide</p>
<p>Save & quit with</p>
<p>Ctrl</p>
<p>+Q.</p>
<p>print("hi")</p>

The reverse conversion writes one <p> per unit, using the <source> text. It does not restore the heading, the <kbd> element or the code fence, and it does not use <target> text. See XLIFF output for the exact rules.

docs.title: Do the same from Python
docs.text:
from vexy_markliff import VexyMarkliff

converter = VexyMarkliff()

markdown = "# Guide\n\nSave & quit with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+Q.\n"
xliff = converter.markdown_to_xliff(markdown, "en", "de")
print(xliff)

restored = converter.xliff_to_markdown(xliff)
print(restored)

markdown_to_xliff returns the XLIFF document as a string. xliff_to_markdown returns the reconstructed text as a string. Neither method reads or writes files.

docs.title: Convert HTML
docs.text:
HTML input works the same way:

vexy-markliff html2xliff page.html page.xlf --source_lang=en --target_lang=fr

The text inside <title> is extracted too, because the parser walks the whole tree, including <head>.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Command line lists every command and flag.
  • Python API documents the classes and exceptions.
  • Troubleshooting explains what to do when the CLI exits with status 1.

docs.title: The CLI exits with status 1 and prints nothing
docs.text:
The CLI catches every exception and calls sys.exit(1). Validation failures happen before any logging, so they leave no message. Check these causes in order:

  1. The input file does not exist. The path is relative to the current directory.

    ls -l guide.md

  2. A language code is invalid. Codes must be two lowercase ASCII letters. EN, en-US, pt_BR and deu all fail.

    vexy-markliff md2xliff guide.md guide.xlf --source_lang=en --target_lang=de

  3. The input is empty or contains only whitespace.

To see the actual exception, call the converter from Python, where it is not swallowed:

from pathlib import Path
from vexy_markliff import VexyMarkliff

text = Path("guide.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
VexyMarkliff().markdown_to_xliff(text, "en", "de")

The traceback names the exception (ValidationError, ConversionError) and its message, for example Invalid target language code: EN.

docs.title: The CLI exits with status 1 and logs a parse error
docs.text:
Errors raised inside the conversion step are logged before the exit, for example:

Failed to parse XLIFF XML: Couldn't find end of Start Tag bad line 1, line 2, column 1 (<string>, line 2)
XLIFF to Markdown conversion failed: Invalid XLIFF XML: ...

The input for xliff2md or xliff2html is not well-formed XML. Check it with an XML validator or python -c "from lxml import etree; etree.parse('file.xlf')".

docs.title: xliff2md writes an empty file
docs.text:
The command succeeded but found no units. The reader looks only for <trans-unit> elements in the namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1. Files from other tools usually use the XLIFF 2.x structure (<unit>, <segment>) or the XLIFF 1.2 namespace (urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:1.2), and both yield zero units.

Only files written by vexy-markliff itself are read correctly. See XLIFF output.

docs.title: The translated text does not appear after converting back
docs.text:
xliff2md and xliff2html use the <source> text of each unit and ignore <target>. This is a limitation of version 1.3. To get the translations out, read the targets with the models:

from pathlib import Path
from vexy_markliff.models.xliff import XLIFFDocument

doc = XLIFFDocument.from_xml(Path("guide.de.xlf").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
for unit in doc.files[0].units:
    print(unit.id, unit.target or unit.source)

docs.title: A sentence is split across several units
docs.text: Inline markup splits text. Save **now** please becomes three units: Save, now, please. The extractor works on lxml text nodes and does not yet use inline codes (<mrk>, <ph>). The planned behaviour is described in HTML mapping rules.

docs.title: Script, style or code text appears in the XLIFF
docs.text: The extractor takes every text node, including <script>, <style>, <pre> and <code> content. Remove such content before conversion, or drop the matching units afterwards.

docs.title: Headings, lists and links are lost on the way back
docs.text: The reverse conversion writes one <p> per unit and has no record of the original element. Keep the original document; version 1.3 cannot rebuild it from the XLIFF.

docs.title: The configuration file has no effect
docs.text:
ConversionConfig.load() reads source_language, target_language and split_sentences from YAML, but the CLI has no option to load it, and the converter does not read the values. Pass language codes as method arguments or CLI flags.

ConversionConfig.load() also returns the default configuration, without raising, when the file is missing or contains an invalid value. If your settings seem ignored when you use it directly, inspect the returned object:

from vexy_markliff import ConversionConfig

config = ConversionConfig.load("vexy-markliff.yaml")
print(config.source_language, config.target_language, config.split_sentences)

docs.title: __version__ is unknown
docs.text: vexy_markliff/__version__.py is generated by hatch-vcs when the package is built or installed. A bare source checkout on sys.path does not have it. Install the package (uv pip install -e .) to generate it.

docs.title: The examples/ scripts fail with ModuleNotFoundError
docs.text: The scripts in examples/ import modules such as vexy_markliff.core.element_classifier and vexy_markliff.core.format_style, which were removed when the code base was simplified. They do not run against version 1.3. Use the snippets in Quick start and Python API instead.

docs.title: Design overview
docs.text:
Specification, not current behaviour

The pages in this section describe how vexy-markliff is meant to work. Most of it is not implemented in version 1.3. For what the code does today, see XLIFF output and Architecture.

These notes were migrated from the project's design documents (originally docs/500-intro.md to docs/540-extras.md and docs/700-sentencing.md) and edited for consistency.

docs.title: Purpose and scope
docs.text:
One sentence: convert Markdown or HTML to XLIFF, and back, with a choice of where the source and target text are stored.

The converter should preserve document structure, inline markup and metadata well enough that a translated XLIFF file can be merged back into an HTML or Markdown document that differs from the original only in its text.

docs.title: Planned pipeline
docs.text:
Markdown ─┐                ┌─► XLIFF units ─┐
          ├─► HTML ─► tree ┤                ├─► merge ─► HTML ─┬─► Markdown
HTML ─────┘                └─► skeleton ────┘                  │
                                                          (optional)
Stage Planned component Parse markdown-it-py (with selected mdit-py-plugins) for Markdown; lxml for HTML Extract Walk the tree, apply the HTML mapping rules, emit units and a skeleton Merge Put translated segments back into the skeleton placeholders Metadata Keep round-trip hints (Markdown markers, alignment keys) on each <unit>

The processing order is: load content, normalize newlines and encoding, render HTML, apply the HTML rules, assemble the XLIFF, write the skeleton.

Validation after extraction: every <ph> references an <originalData> entry, and every <unit> carries fs:fs.

docs.title: One-document mode
docs.text:
The input is one document. A storage switch decides where its text goes:

Storage Segment layout source (default) <segment><source>text</source></segment> target <segment><target>text</target></segment> both <segment><source>text</source><target>text</target></segment>

docs.title: Two-document mode
docs.text:
The input is a source document and an existing translation.

  1. Structural alignment. Match headings and list positions between the two documents by walking both trees in the same order.
  2. Sentence alignment. Split paragraphs with the same segmentation rules on both sides.
  3. Fallback. If the structures diverge, pair blocks in sequence and add a <note> with an alignment warning.
  4. Result. Segments with both sides filled get state="translated".

docs.title: Planned command line
docs.text:
vexy-markliff md2xliff INPUT OUTPUT [--mode=one-doc|two-doc] [--storage=source|target|both]
                                    [--target-file=FILE] [--src-lang=BCP47] [--trg-lang=BCP47]
                                    [--extensions=tables,footnotes,...] [--split-sentences]
vexy-markliff html2xliff INPUT OUTPUT [same switches]
vexy-markliff xliff2md INPUT OUTPUT [--respect-markdown-style]
vexy-markliff xliff2html INPUT OUTPUT
vexy-markliff batch-convert --input-dir DIR --output-dir DIR [--pattern '*.md'] [--parallel N]

Skeleton files would be written next to the XLIFF (--skeleton-dir, default ./skeletons). Language codes would accept full BCP 47 tags.

Note

In version 1.3 only md2xliff, html2xliff, xliff2md and xliff2html exist, with --source_lang and --target_lang. See Command line.

docs.title: Planned configuration
docs.text:
source_language: en
target_language: es
mode: one-doc
storage: source
extensions: [tables, footnotes, task_lists, strikethrough]
split_sentences: true
skeleton_dir: ./skeletons
preserve_whitespace: true

with environment overrides VEXY_MARKLIFF_CONFIG, VEXY_MARKLIFF_SRC_LANG, VEXY_MARKLIFF_TRG_LANG and VEXY_MARKLIFF_SKELETON_DIR.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Every converter function has a test that checks structure (presence of fs:fs) and content (round-trip equality).
  • Fixtures cover tables, task lists, front matter, raw HTML, forms, media and ruby text.
  • markdown → xliff → markdown and html → xliff → html are byte-stable apart from whitespace normalization.
  • Two-document mode reports alignment warnings when paragraph counts differ.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text: Page Content XLIFF 2.1 primer The XLIFF structure the design targets, inline codes, ITS 2.0, a worked example HTML mapping rules How each HTML element maps to units, groups, markers and placeholders Markdown mapping rules How Markdown constructs map through HTML to XLIFF, and what metadata keeps the round trip lossless Sentence segmentation Segmentation policy and candidate libraries Libraries and tools Third-party libraries and formats referenced by the design Sample files One passage in XLIFF, PO, TS and RESX

docs.title: HTML mapping rules
docs.text:
Specification

These rules describe the planned extractor. Version 1.3 extracts plain text nodes only; see XLIFF output.

The rules decide, for every HTML5 element, whether it stays in the skeleton, becomes a <unit> or <group>, becomes an inline <mrk>, or becomes a <ph> placeholder. All of them rely on the Format Style attributes fs:fs and fs:subFs to remember the original element and its attributes.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Every generated <xliff> root declares:

<xliff xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0"
       xmlns:fs="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:fs:2.0"
       version="2.1" srcLang="en" trgLang="de">

docs.title: Attribute encoding in fs:subFs
docs.text:
HTML attributes are stored as name/value pairs:

  • , separates a name from its value: href,https://example.com.
  • \ separates pairs: class,hero\id,lead.
  • A literal comma is written \,; a literal backslash \\.
  • An empty value is written name,.

So <a href="https://example.com" target="_blank"> becomes fs:fs="a" fs:subFs="href,https://example.com\target,_blank".

Verbatim HTML fragments go into <originalData><data id="…">…</data></originalData>, as CDATA where the fragment contains < or &, to avoid double escaping.

docs.title: Document skeleton
docs.text:
Elements: <!DOCTYPE>, html, head, body, base, link, meta, script, style, noscript, template.

These stay in the skeleton file referenced by <file><skeleton href="…"/>. Placeholders such as ###u17### mark where units go back in. Only text inside child elements described below (for example <title>) is promoted to units.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>###u1###</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css" />
  </head>
  <body class="landing">###u2###</body>
</html>

docs.title: Sectioning and grouping
docs.text:
Elements: article, aside, details, dialog, div, fieldset, figure, figcaption, footer, header, main, menu, nav, section, summary.

  • Wrap each section in a <group> or <unit> with fs:fs set to the element name and attributes in fs:subFs.
  • Keep purely structural wrappers (a <div> that holds only blocks) in the skeleton and promote only the child blocks.
  • Promote text-bearing elements (figcaption, summary, dialog) to units.
<group id="nav" fs:fs="nav" fs:subFs="class,main-menu">
  <unit id="nav-title" fs:fs="h2">
    <segment><source>Site navigation</source></segment>
  </unit>
</group>

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
Elements: ul, ol, li, menu, dl, dt, dd.

  • Each list container becomes a <group> with fs:fs set to the container element.
  • Each li, dt and dd becomes a child <unit>.
  • List attributes (start, type, reversed, value) go into fs:subFs.
  • Nested lists become nested groups.
<group id="faq" fs:fs="dl">
  <unit id="q1" fs:fs="dt"><segment><source>What is Markliff?</source></segment></unit>
  <unit id="a1" fs:fs="dd"><segment><source>It is our HTML to XLIFF bridge.</source></segment></unit>
</group>

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Elements: table, caption, colgroup, col, thead, tbody, tfoot, tr, th, td.

  • By default keep the whole table in one <unit fs:fs="table" xml:space="preserve">, with table attributes in fs:subFs.
  • When cells must be translated one by one, break the table into child units and keep the outer markup in <originalData>.
<unit id="pricing" fs:fs="table" fs:subFs="class,pricing" xml:space="preserve">
  <segment>
    <source><![CDATA[<table class="pricing"><thead><tr><th>Plan</th><th>Price</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody><tr><td>Starter</td><td>$9</td></tr></tbody></table>]]></source>
  </segment>
</unit>

docs.title: Text blocks and headings
docs.text:
Elements: address, blockquote, caption, h1–h6, hgroup, legend, p, pre, title.

  • Each becomes a <unit> with fs:fs set to the element name.
  • pre gets xml:space="preserve".
  • title text is a unit; its position is a skeleton placeholder.
  • hgroup becomes a <group fs:fs="hgroup"> around its heading units.

Segmentation inside these units:

  • An <s> element is one <segment> and is never split.
  • A <p> is split into sentences, one <segment> per sentence. See Sentence segmentation.
  • Other blocks are one segment unless the HTML already carries <s> elements.

docs.title: Inline text semantics
docs.text:
Elements: a, abbr, b, bdi, bdo, cite, code, data, del, dfn, em, i, ins, kbd, label, mark, output, q, ruby, rb, rp, rt, rtc, s, samp, small, span, strong, sub, sup, time, u, var.

  • Each becomes a <mrk> inside the surrounding segment, with fs:fs set to the element and its attributes (href, datetime, title, aria-* and so on) in fs:subFs.
  • Nesting is kept as it appears; the merger replays it.
  • ins and del keep change metadata such as datetime.
  • ruby, rb, rt, rp and rtc stay grouped so that ruby layout can be rebuilt.
  • lang, dir and translate stay on the marker. bdi and bdo always keep dir; if it is absent, record dir,auto.
<segment>
  <source>View the <mrk id="m1" fs:fs="a" fs:subFs="href,https://example.com\target,_blank">documentation</mrk>
    updated on <mrk id="m2" fs:fs="time" fs:subFs="datetime,2024-05-12">May 12</mrk>.</source>
</segment>

docs.title: Void elements and placeholders
docs.text:
Elements: area, base, br, col, embed, hr, img, input, link, meta, param, source, track, wbr.

  • Each occurrence becomes <ph> with dataRef pointing to an <originalData> entry that holds the literal HTML.
  • base, link and meta normally stay in the skeleton; the placeholder rule covers them when they appear in mixed content, for example raw HTML in Markdown.
  • Placeholder ids are deterministic (for example ph-img-001) so that the merger can match them.
<unit id="hero-copy" fs:fs="p">
  <originalData>
    <data id="img1"><img src="hero.png" alt="Dashboard screenshot" width="640" height="320"/></data>
    <data id="br1"><br/></data>
  </originalData>
  <segment>
    <source><ph id="ph-img1" dataRef="img1"/> Experience Markliff today.<ph id="ph-br1" dataRef="br1"/></source>
  </segment>
</unit>

docs.title: Embedded media
docs.text:
Elements: audio, video, canvas, iframe, map, object, picture, svg, math, and their children area, source, track, param.

  • Self-contained widgets (iframe, canvas, object, svg, math) are stored whole in a <unit xml:space="preserve">. SVG and MathML internals are never rewritten.
  • picture is a unit; its source children are <originalData> entries.
  • map is a unit; each area is a placeholder inside it.
  • audio and video mirror their nesting: source and track become placeholders, transcripts become child units.
<unit id="product-video" fs:fs="video" fs:subFs="controls,\width,640" xml:space="preserve">
  <originalData>
    <data id="src-main"><source src="promo.mp4" type="video/mp4"/></data>
    <data id="trk-en"><track kind="subtitles" src="promo-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default></data>
  </originalData>
  <segment>
    <source><ph id="ph-src1" dataRef="src-main"/><ph id="ph-trk1" dataRef="trk-en"/></source>
  </segment>
</unit>

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Elements: form, button, datalist, fieldset, input, label, legend, meter, optgroup, option, output, progress, select, textarea.

  • A whole form is kept as one <unit xml:space="preserve"> so that validation attributes survive.
  • Visible text inside it (label, button captions, option text) becomes separate units referenced by placeholders.
  • Void controls (input, meter, progress) are placeholders inside the form unit.
  • Markdown task-list checkboxes use the same placeholder rule.
<unit id="contact-form" fs:fs="form" fs:subFs="action,/submit\method,POST" xml:space="preserve">
  <segment>
    <source><![CDATA[<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <label for="name">###u-name###</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required>
  <button type="submit">###u-submit###</button>
</form>]]></source>
  </segment>
</unit>
<unit id="u-name" fs:fs="label"><segment><source>Name</source></segment></unit>
<unit id="u-submit" fs:fs="button"><segment><source>Send</source></segment></unit>

docs.title: Scripts, templates and custom elements
docs.text:
• script stays in the skeleton. Inline JavaScript is not translated; extract user-facing strings from it (for example from JSON) before conversion.
  • noscript fallback text becomes a unit; the tag stays in the skeleton.
  • template stays in the skeleton unless it contains fallback text, which is then promoted.
  • slot and slot="…" are recorded in fs:subFs; fallback text in slots is ordinary inline content.
  • Custom elements (any name with a hyphen, such as app-shell or geo-map) are treated as inline or block elements depending on their content, with the literal tag name in fs:fs.

docs.title: Deprecated elements
docs.text: acronym, applet, basefont, big, blink, center, dir, font, frame, frameset, isindex, marquee, menuitem, noframes, strike and tt are kept as written and handled like their modern counterparts (for example center like div). Their visible text is still extracted.

docs.title: Attributes that matter for localization
docs.text:
Most attributes are carried through fs:subFs untouched. A few carry text or localization instructions:

Attribute Relevance lang Language of the content (BCP 47 tag); must change in the target dir ltr, rtl or auto; matters for mixed-direction text translate yes or no; maps to ITS Translate title Tooltip text, often the expansion of an <abbr>; translatable alt Text alternative of an image; translatable aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-labelledby Accessible names and descriptions; aria-label is translatable text cite, datetime On blockquote, q, del, ins: source URL and ISO 8601 time data-* Script data; not translatable

docs.title: Element reference
docs.text: Elements Handling <!DOCTYPE>, html, head, body Skeleton; child text promoted to units base, link, meta Skeleton; inline occurrences become <ph> title Unit fs:fs="title", placeholder in skeleton style, script Skeleton only noscript, template Skeleton; fallback text promoted article, aside, main, nav, section Group or unit with fs:fs and attributes header, footer, div Skeleton wrapper; text children promoted figure, figcaption Figure as group or unit; caption as unit details, summary, dialog Block kept with fs:fs; text children as units fieldset, legend Fieldset as group; legend as unit menu, ul, ol, li List group and item units dl, dt, dd Definition-list group, term and definition units p, address, blockquote, pre, caption Units; paragraphs split into sentences h1–h6, hgroup Units; hgroup as wrapping group span, mark, strong, em, i, b, u, small, s <mrk> cite, q, dfn, abbr, var, code, kbd, samp <mrk> time, data, output, label <mrk> with value attributes sub, sup, bdi, bdo, ruby, rb, rt, rp, rtc <mrk> with direction and ruby data del, ins <mrk> with change metadata hr, br, wbr <ph> table and its parts Preserved unit, or nested groups for cell-level work colgroup, col Inside the preserved table markup form Preserved unit; text children as units button Unit input, textarea, select, meter, progress Placeholders inside the form unit option, optgroup, datalist Units for visible captions img, picture, source, track <ph> inside media units audio, video Units; sources and tracks as placeholders map, area Map as unit; areas as placeholders iframe, embed, object, param Unit with full markup canvas, svg, math Preserved unit; internals untouched slot, custom elements Structure kept; fallback text promoted; tag name in fs:fs

docs.title: Validation checklist
docs.text:
• Every unit created from HTML has fs:fs matching the original element.
  • Every <ph> refers to an existing <data id="…">.
  • Each <s> maps to exactly one <segment>; paragraphs are sentence-split.
  • When in doubt, check against the OASIS XLIFF 2.1 specification.

docs.title: Markdown mapping rules
docs.text:
Specification

These rules describe the planned behaviour. Version 1.3 renders Markdown to HTML and extracts plain text nodes; it records no round-trip metadata.

Markdown is never mapped to XLIFF directly. It is rendered to HTML first, and the HTML goes through the HTML mapping rules. This keeps one set of extraction rules for both input formats. What Markdown adds is metadata: the information needed to write Markdown, not just HTML, after translation.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Parse. markdown-it-py turns the Markdown into a token stream.
  2. Render. The tokens are rendered to deterministic HTML5.
  3. Extract. The HTML rules produce units, groups, markers and placeholders.
  4. Record hints. Markdown-specific details are stored on each unit so the merger can rebuild the original syntax.

Version 1.3 performs steps 1 and 2 with the CommonMark preset plus the table and strikethrough rules, and with raw HTML enabled.

docs.title: Block constructs
Inline constructs
Raw HTML and custom syntax
docs.text:
• Raw HTML inside Markdown skips Markdown processing and goes straight to the HTML rules.
  • Extensions that emit custom elements (<note-box>, <callout>) follow the custom-element rule in HTML mapping rules.
  • When inline HTML introduces new block boundaries, the HTML segmentation decides the units.

docs.title: Round-trip metadata
docs.text:
To write Markdown, not HTML, after translation, each unit records (in <notes> or in extra fs:subFs keys):

Construct What to record Emphasis * or _, and the marker length for strong emphasis Code fences Fence characters (``` or ~~~) and the info string Links Inline or reference style; reference labels and definitions Task items The original [ ] or [x] token and whether the box was disabled Tables Column alignment markers (:---, :---:, ---:) Front matter The original serialization (YAML, TOML or JSON), verbatim

docs.title: Errors and fallbacks
docs.text:
• HTML outside the mapped set is logged and treated as literal text inside a segment, with an extraction note.
  • HTML entities are unescaped by the renderer; the XLIFF writer must not escape them twice.
  • Extensions that inject <script> or <style> must be disabled or explicitly allowed. Executable content is never localized.

docs.title: Test checklist
docs.text:
• Render Markdown fixtures to HTML and compare with stored HTML snapshots before testing extraction.
  • Every generated unit has fs:fs matching its HTML element.
  • markdown → XLIFF → markdown round trips cover headings, lists, tables, code fences, task lists and footnotes.
  • The recorded metadata reproduces the original Markdown syntax when merging back.

docs.title: Sample files
docs.text:
The same passage, the opening of Franz Kafka's Die Verwandlung in German with an English translation, stored in four localization formats. Use them to compare how each format pairs source and target text, and as test input when you work on readers for other formats.

File Format Source/target pairing 609-samsa.xlf.xml XLIFF 2 <unit> per paragraph, <segment> per sentence, <source> and <target> 610-samsa.po.txt GNU gettext PO msgid (German) and msgstr (English) per sentence 611-samsa.ts.xml Qt Linguist TS <message> with <source> and <translation> inside a <context> 612-samsa.resx.xml .NET RESX <data> per sentence; English in <value>, German in <comment>

The files carry .xml and .txt extensions so that a browser displays them instead of downloading them.

docs.title: XLIFF sample in detail
docs.text:
The XLIFF file shows the structure the design targets: one <unit> per paragraph and one <segment> per sentence, with the language pair on <file>:

<file id="samsa" srcLang="de" trgLang="en">
  <unit id="p2">
    <segment>
      <source>»Was ist mit mir geschehen?« dachte er.</source>
      <target>“What’s happened to me?” he thought.</target>
    </segment>
    <segment>
      <source>Es war kein Traum.</source>
      <target>It wasn’t a dream.</target>
    </segment>
  </unit>
</file>

Two details to notice:

  • The sentences keep their own punctuation and quotation marks (»…« in German, “…” in English). A segmenter must not strip them.
  • The file declares the namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.1 and puts srcLang/trgLang on <file>. The XLIFF 2.1 standard uses the namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0 and puts srcLang/trgLang on the <xliff> root.

docs.title: Reading the sample with version 1.3
docs.text:
vexy-markliff xliff2html 609-samsa.xlf.xml samsa.html

The command exits with status 0 and writes an empty samsa.html, because the version 1.3 reader looks only for <trans-unit> elements. See XLIFF output.

docs.title: Sentence segmentation
docs.text:
Specification and research notes

Version 1.3 does not split sentences. A paragraph without inline markup becomes one unit. vexy_markliff.utils.split_sentences_simple exists but is not called by the converter.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
The HTML mapping rules set three rules:

  1. An <s> element is one <segment>. It is never split further.
  2. A <p> element is split into sentences, one <segment> per sentence, all inside the paragraph's <unit>.
  3. Other block elements stay one segment unless the HTML already marks sentences with <s>.

XLIFF allows segmentation to change later, inside the unit, so the splitter's job is a good first guess, not a final answer.

docs.title: Why a regular expression is not enough
docs.text:
split_sentences_simple splits on runs of ., ! and ?:

>>> from vexy_markliff.utils import split_sentences_simple
>>> split_sentences_simple("Dr. Who? Yes. New sentence.")
['Dr', 'Who', 'Yes', 'New sentence']

It breaks after abbreviations and drops the punctuation that translators need. A usable splitter must handle abbreviations, numbers (p. 55), quotations, and scripts that use other terminators, such as 。 in Chinese and Japanese or । in Hindi.

docs.title: Reference: Unicode text segmentation
docs.text: Unicode Standard Annex #29, Unicode Text Segmentation, defines default boundaries for grapheme clusters, words and sentences. Its sentence rules work on character properties (STerm, ATerm, Close, Sp and others) and are the baseline that ICU and most libraries tailor. The default rules do not know about abbreviations, which is why the libraries below add language-specific rules or models.

docs.title: Candidate libraries
docs.text:
The project's research compared these Python options. Check each project's licence, language coverage and maintenance status before adopting one.

Library Approach Notes from the research pySBD Rule-based (port of the Ruby pragmatic segmenter) Deterministic, about 22 languages, good on messy text such as OCR and email syntok Rule-based, pure Python Small and fast; aimed at Indo-European languages sentencex Rule-based with language fallbacks (Wikimedia) Wide language coverage wtpsplit ("Segment any Text") Transformer models Many languages; handles missing punctuation; can be adapted to a domain Stanza Neural pipeline per language Accurate; heavier dependency spaCy sentencizer (rule-based) or dependency parser sentencizer is fast; the parser is slower and model-dependent NLTK Punkt Unsupervised model Common baseline for European languages BlingFire Compiled finite-state models Fast; platform-dependent binaries

Rule-based splitters are fast, offline and deterministic, which suits a converter that must give the same output every time. Model-based splitters cope better with unusual text at the cost of large dependencies.

pySBD can also run as a spaCy pipeline component, so a project that already uses spaCy can swap segmenters without changing the rest of its pipeline.

docs.title: Marking boundaries in text
docs.text: When a language model inserts sentence boundaries, the research notes suggest the Unicode pair U+2E28 LEFT DOUBLE PARENTHESIS ⸨ and U+2E29 RIGHT DOUBLE PARENTHESIS ⸩ as delimiters: they are rare in natural text, are a matched open/close pair in Unicode, and do not collide with Markdown or HTML syntax. A marked paragraph looks like ⸨My name is Jonas E. Smith.⸩ ⸨Please turn to p. 55.⸩.

docs.title: Libraries and tools
docs.text: The design builds on a few third-party libraries and specifications. This page records what each one contributes and which parts the project uses or plans to use.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Specification Relevance OASIS XLIFF Version 2.1 (OASIS Standard, 13 February 2018) Target format: core elements, inline codes, Format Style module, ITS integration. Core namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0. W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) 2.0 Localization metadata in HTML (translate, notes, terminology), mapped into XLIFF 2.1 Unicode Standard Annex #29 Default sentence boundaries; see Sentence segmentation CommonMark The Markdown dialect markdown-it-py implements

docs.title: markdown-it-py
docs.text:
A Python port of the JavaScript markdown-it parser. It is CommonMark compliant, produces a token stream that can be inspected or changed before rendering, and supports presets (commonmark, gfm-like, zero) and plugins.

Version 1.3 uses it as follows (see core/parser.py):

import markdown_it

md = markdown_it.MarkdownIt("commonmark", {"breaks": True, "html": True})
md.enable(["table", "strikethrough"])
html = md.render(text)

markdown-it-py renders to HTML only; it has no Markdown writer. Writing Markdown after translation therefore needs the round-trip metadata described in Markdown mapping rules.

docs.title: mdit-py-plugins
docs.text:
The companion package for markdown-it-py extensions. The design plans to use these (not yet a dependency):

Plugin Adds Front matter YAML or TOML metadata block at the start of the document Footnotes Reference and inline footnotes Definition lists Pandoc-style term/definition lists Task lists [ ] and [x] checkboxes in list items Attributes {#id .class} attributes on elements Containers, colon fences Custom fenced blocks Heading anchors id attributes on headings

docs.title: lxml
docs.text:
Parses HTML (lxml.html.fromstring) and builds and parses XLIFF (lxml.etree). Reading units out of a standard XLIFF 2 file with lxml looks like this:

from lxml import etree

ns = {"x": "urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0"}
root = etree.fromstring(xliff_bytes)
for unit in root.iterfind(".//x:unit", ns):
    for segment in unit.iterfind("x:segment", ns):
        source = segment.find("x:source", ns)
        target = segment.find("x:target", ns)
        print(unit.get("id"), source.text, target.text if target is not None else None)

docs.title: Translate Toolkit
docs.text:
A Python toolkit with converters between localization formats and quality checks. It is useful next to vexy-markliff when a translation vendor needs a different format:

Task Command PO to XLIFF po2xliff messages.de.po messages.de.xlf XLIFF to PO xliff2po messages.de.xlf messages.de.po Markdown to a PO template md2po README.md README.pot

docs.title: Other formats
docs.text:
XLIFF is one of several bilingual formats. Plural forms are not native to XLIFF; the usual practice is to embed ICU MessageFormat inside the segment and let the tooling parse both layers:

<unit id="file_count">
  <notes><note>Pluralized string (# substituted)</note></notes>
  <segment>
    <source>{count, plural, one {# file} other {# files}}</source>
    <target>{count, plural, one {# plik} few {# pliki} other {# plików}}</target>
  </segment>
</unit>

See Sample files for the same text in XLIFF, PO, Qt TS and RESX.

docs.title: XLIFF 2.1 primer
docs.text:
XLIFF (XML Localization Interchange File Format) is the OASIS standard for passing translatable text between tools. Version 2.1 became an OASIS Standard on 13 February 2018. It keeps the 2.0 core and adds, among other things, normative support for the W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) 2.0.

This page summarizes the parts of XLIFF 2.1 that the vexy-markliff design relies on.

docs.title: Extraction and merge
docs.text:
An XLIFF workflow is a round trip:

  1. An extractor reads the original document, separates translatable text from structure, and writes an XLIFF file plus, optionally, a skeleton.
  2. Translators fill in <target> elements in a CAT tool, which protects the inline codes.
  3. A merger puts the translated text back into the structure and writes the translated document.

The XLIFF file is a bitext: source and translation side by side, organized into units.

docs.title: Core structure
docs.text:
Element Role <xliff> Root. Attributes version (2.1), srcLang (required) and trgLang (required once any <target> exists). Namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0. <file> Everything extracted from one original document. id is required; original names the source file. <skeleton> The non-translatable remainder of the original, embedded or referenced with href. <group> Optional container for units that mirror nested structure, for example a list. <unit> One logical block of text, such as a paragraph, heading or list item. Tools must not change the unit structure. <segment> One source/target pair inside a unit. A unit can hold several segments, for example one per sentence. Segmentation may change during translation. <source>, <target> The text, including inline codes. <notes> / <note> Comments for translators. <originalData> / <data> The original markup that inline codes refer to.

The split between a fixed <unit> structure and flexible <segment> boundaries is what lets a merger rebuild the document reliably while still allowing sentence-level translation.

docs.title: Inline codes
docs.text:
XLIFF 1.2 used <bpt>, <ept>, <ph> and <it>. XLIFF 2.x replaces them with three elements:

Element Purpose Content Typical HTML or Markdown <ph> Placeholder for a standalone code Empty, e.g. <ph id="1" dataRef="d1"/> <img>, <br>, <hr>, Markdown --- <pc> Paired code around text Text and nested codes <b>…</b>, <a href="…">…</a>, **bold** <mrk> Annotation of a span Text and nested codes translate="no", terminology

vexy-markliff deliberately uses <mrk> with Format Style attributes for inline HTML elements, and <ph> for void elements. It does not use <pc> or dataRefStart/dataRefEnd. See HTML mapping rules.

docs.title: Format Style module
docs.text:
The Format Style module (namespace urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:fs:2.0) adds two attributes that let a tool rebuild a preview of the original:

  • fs:fs names the original element, for example p, h1 or a.
  • fs:subFs carries its attributes as name/value pairs, for example href,https://example.com.

The design uses these attributes as the record of the original markup on <unit>, <group> and <mrk> elements. The escaping rules are in HTML mapping rules.

docs.title: ITS 2.0
docs.text:
ITS 2.0 is a W3C Recommendation for localization metadata in XML and HTML. XLIFF 2.1 maps several of its data categories:

ITS data category In HTML In XLIFF 2.1 Translate translate="no" Block level: translate="no" on <unit>. Inline: <mrk translate="no">. Preserve Space xml:space="preserve", <pre> xml:space="preserve" on the unit Localization Note ITS note markup <note> inside the unit's <notes> Terminology, Allowed Characters, Storage Size ITS attributes Carried through to the matching XLIFF modules

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Input index.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <title>Welcome</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Product Information</h1>
    <p>Please visit <a href="https://example.com">our website</a> for more details.</p>
</body>
</html>

Skeleton skeleton/index.skl.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <title>###u1###</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>###u2###</h1>
    <p>###u3###</p>
</body>
</html>

XLIFF after translation into Spanish:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<xliff xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:2.0"
       xmlns:fs="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:fs:2.0"
       version="2.1" srcLang="en" trgLang="es">
  <file id="f1" original="index.html">
    <skeleton href="skeleton/index.skl.html"/>
    <unit id="u1" fs:fs="title">
      <segment>
        <source>Welcome</source>
        <target>Bienvenido</target>
      </segment>
    </unit>
    <unit id="u2" fs:fs="h1">
      <segment>
        <source>Product Information</source>
        <target>Información del producto</target>
      </segment>
    </unit>
    <unit id="u3" fs:fs="p">
      <segment>
        <source>Please visit <mrk id="m1" fs:fs="a"
          fs:subFs="href,https://example.com">our website</mrk> for more details.</source>
        <target>Visite <mrk id="m1" fs:fs="a"
          fs:subFs="href,https://example.com">nuestro sitio web</mrk> para más detalles.</target>
      </segment>
    </unit>
  </file>
</xliff>

The merger replaces ###u1### to ###u3### with the target text and rebuilds the <a> element from the <mrk> attributes.

Compare this with what version 1.3 writes today in XLIFF output.
